newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FOCUS-RBNZ okays NZ easing but warns of exuberance.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-RBNZ okays NZ easing but warns of exuberance.

text.p: Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash on Tuesday formally endorsed New Zealand's recent easing of monetary conditions but warned markets of over-exuberance.
In a major set piece to markets, Brash released the bank's six-monthly monetary policy statement (MPS) predicting a lower inflation track but also lower growth.

But much of the information was dated as the MPS was finalised before the formation last week of the new National-New Zealand First coalition government, one of whose first acts was to relax the RB's inflation target and add sustainable growth as
a separate goal.
"On balance, it is the bank's judgement that some easing in monetary conditions compared with those assumed in the Monetary Policy Statement is indeed appropriate," Brash told a news conference.
"But it is also our judgement that the initial easing in conditions which occurred in reaction to last week's developments was somewhat excessive," Brash said.

In the markets, short-term interest rates, which had rallied nearly 200 basis points since the October 12 election, initially rose around 20 basis points to 7.95 percent, and the New Zealand dollar jumped over half a U.S. cent to 70.5 cents.
"What we've seen is an easing in monetary conditions, but generally speaking, not as significant an easing as the market would have expected," said Westpac economist Hamish Macalister.

The easing was welcomed by new Treasurer Winston Peters, who is also now Brash's boss. He had made clear his view before the election that the New Zealand dollar was overvalued and conditions were too tight.

"Overall the governor (Brash) is accepting the easing in conditions that have followed the coalition announcement which is pleasing for exporters and home owners," Peters, who was appointed Treasurer last week, said in a statement.

Peters, who widened the bank's inflation target to 0-3 percent from 0-2 percent, said he would not be in the habit of commenting on the RB's statement and that day-to-day management of monetary conditions was "the governor's business".
Labour Party finance spokesperson Michael Cullen predicted interest rates and the currency would rise as a result of Brash's statements and said Peters' honeymoon was already over.

"We have in this new government the worst of both worlds -- a substantial fiscal loosening and a continued refusal to invest in the economy's ability to sustain strong levels of economic growth. The message for exporters is clear -- the pain is not over," Cullen said.

Cullen said the bank's short-term outlook for growth was pessimistic -- 1.3 percent in the March 1997 year rising to 2.6 percent the following year -- and noted it was below the bank's estimate of sustainable growth at 2.75 percent.
Brash said growth in the last quarter of 1996 and the first of 1997 was predicted to be slightly stronger than previously projected, but it would remain subdued.

That would help annual inflation fall from 2.34 percent in the June year. It is predicted to hold around current levels for two quarters and then fall rapidly to be under 0.5 percent from the March 1998 year and beyond.
But Brash acknowledged there were many uncertainties, particularly pertaining to the new government and its plans to loosen the fiscal stance.
"Looking ahead...there are still considerable uncertainties facing us," he said. Brash cited the fiscal situation and recent housing, import and monetary aggregates data as warning signs.
Economists generally viewed Brash's comments as very cautious.
"A very cautious statement. They have erred on the side of chasing credibility, having suffered shifting from a 0-2 percent to 0-3 percent," said National Bank chief economist Adrian Orr.
-- Wellington newsroom 64 4 4734 746
